subject: music
title: Screen Score Application: Composers & Iconic Themes
welcome_lead: Meet the giants — Williams, Zimmer, Uematsu and Kondo — and the techniques behind their unforgettable themes.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Film & Game Music Adventure 2: applying knowledge of John Williams, Hans Zimmer, Nobuo Uematsu and Koji Kondo's scoring techniques.
final_note: You can identify a Williams, Zimmer or Uematsu cue within seconds.

concepts.def: US composer: Star Wars (1977), Jaws (1975), Harry Potter.
German composer: Inception, The Lion King, Dune.
Japanese composer of Final Fantasy soundtracks.
Nintendo composer — Super Mario and Zelda themes.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Williams uses leitmotif, full symphonic orchestra and unforgettable opening bars. Jaws (1975) — a two-note semitone ostinato signals danger. Star Wars (1977) — heroic brass fanfares for adventure.

His writing channels late-Romantic composers (Wagner, Strauss, Holst) into modern blockbusters.

Zimmer blends orchestra with electronics and percussion. The famous 'BRAAAM' from Inception (2010) became a Hollywood cliché. He uses ostinato pulses, sustained drones and prepared piano.

For The Dark Knight, he built tension with two notes a semitone apart — minimal yet menacing.

Nobuo Uematsu composed sweeping orchestral scores for the Final Fantasy series (1987–), proving game music could match film in depth.

Koji Kondo wrote Nintendo's most famous themes — Super Mario Bros (1985) and The Legend of Zelda (1986). His 8-bit melodies are catchy enough to remain iconic for decades.
